title: Existentialism’s 21st‑Century Continuations - Environmental Philosophy & Eco‑Existentialism
content_html:
Existentialism’s 21st‑Century Continuations - Environmental Philosophy & Eco‑Existentialism

  • Substrate: Ecological/landscape memory; social‑ecological memory as a physical and communal substrate for human memory.
  • Language / Expression: Collective memory, narrative, and ritual responses to climate loss; publicly shared meaning‑making.
  • Meaning / Void / Infinite: Eco‑existential anxiety, grief, and authenticity; intergenerational responsibility as existential stance.

Solastalgia

place‑based distress as memory injury

Solastalgia names the distress of staying in a transforming home landscape, where one’s place memory no longer matches the altered present. It is a mirror image of nostalgia (pain from separation) but arises in situ as environmental change erodes the continuity of autobiographical and communal memory.

  • Definition and clinical framing: see Albrecht’s 2007 paper and recent updates contextualising “spirit of place.” (PubMed; PubMed 2024)
  • Implication: loss of environmental continuity destabilises the Reconstruct phase; existential response is meaning‑making within loss.

Environmental Generational Amnesia (EGA)

shifting baselines in collective memory

EGA describes how each generation normalises a more degraded environment as “baseline,” attenuating collective memory and expectations of biodiversity and air/water quality. This is a direct challenge to existential authenticity because the past remembered is systematically narrowed.

  • Core concept (Kahn, 2002) with accessible overviews and humanities engagements. (PDF; BrainFacts 2023; Memory Studies Review 2024)
  • Implication: append EGA checks to memory‑workflows (e.g., intergenerational interviews; archival photo comparison) before narrative reconstruction.

Social‑ecological memory (SEM)

communities as memory media

SEM denotes the collective repository of practices, stories, and artifacts that encode ecological knowledge for future resilience. It is a substrate for human memory and meaning, linking household, community, and landscape.

  • Recent reviews and applications: Cardoso 2025; Hsu 2025; Khalighi 2022.
  • Implication: treat SEM as an externalized hippocampus for communities; design rituals/archives to keep practices retrievable across generations.

Eco‑anxiety & ecological grief

memory, rumination, and anticipatory loss

Meta‑analytic and review work shows robust associations between climate anxiety and mental health outcomes, while philosophical analyses frame these emotions as existential responses to loss and finitude.

  • Evidence: meta‑analyses and reviews (Kühner 2025; Gago 2024; Annual Review of Clinical Psychology 2024; Cosh 2024).
  • Process models and public emotion: Pihkala 2022; Varutti 2023; Nairn 2023.
  • Implication for memory: anticipatory memory (imagined futures) and rumination patterns can be redirected via community rituals and action‑based meaning.

Slow violence & narrative memory

making the invisible visible

“Slow violence” names harms that unfold gradually and out of sight, challenging the representation of environmental trauma in public memory. Narrative, art, and ritual become existential tools for remembrance and responsibility.

  • Core text: Rob Nixon’s Slow Violence and the Environmentalism of the Poor (2011) and summaries/excerpts. (HUP page; JSTOR; PDF excerpt).
  • Implication: adopt slow‑time exhibits (photo pairs, timelines, testimony) to counteract EGA and embed long‑horizon memory in practice.
